## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
A one-day course in four parts of 90 minutes, on the cohabitation case
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-85}
1. Credibility and tools – science, its crisis, and the toolchain
2. The claim, its estimand and its causal graph – the paper, the five analysts, and who cohabits at all
3. Reproduction and exploration – a recorded result reproduced and questioned, and the specification menu
4. Multiverse, replication and preregistration – the curve, the two replications, one preregistered analysis
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave with: a reproduced result, and what it rests on; an estimand statement and a causal graph of your own; a preregistered analysis; your results on a live class multiverse
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
Work along in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), solo or in pairs, with the browser lab page, a demonstration of every task, as the fallback
:::

::: notes
Welcome – good to have you here. A full day, in four parts of ninety minutes. The first part sets up everything else: what we are doing when we do social science, why people say it is in crisis, what open research proposes to do about it, and the software without which none of it happens. The second part goes inside one published study, built on the National Survey of Family Growth, which asked whether American couples who live together unmarried have become less likely to marry, and asks what question its claim actually answers. In the third you reproduce a result that one of five independent analysts reported for that claim, find out what it rests on, and then vary the analysis yourself. And in the fourth we read what the class built, look at two replications, and settle on the one analysis you would publish.
:::
